about: Where version 6's shell syntax intends another reading than the reference parser (mvdan.cc/sh), each family of lines is named here with its reason (doc 21 revision 3, section 35: decisions alter an expectation with evidence; they are not ignored failures). A difference is explained only when its two outcomes and its source match one family.

decisions.reason: Bash reads @( !( *( ?( +( patterns only with the extglob option on, and it is off by default; version 6 reads the default grammar, so such a line is invalid as bash would say.

Version 6 refuses a loop, conditional, case, function or array whole without checking every token of its body; the reference rejects the same line as invalid. Both readings refuse the line, so admission is the same.

bash -n accepts these lines; they fail only when run (let with spaced operands, eval of an array, a command word such as ENV["X"]). Version 6 follows bash's grammar, and classification still refuses what it cannot place.
Bash rejects a reserved word where a command should start; the reference reads it as a plain word.

The line turns extglob on with shopt and then uses an extended glob; version 6 reads every line with the default grammar, since a shell option set in the same line cannot change how the line was already parsed by bash either.

After a ; a } stands where a command starts, so bash reads it as the reserved word closing a group that was never opened and rejects the line (awk programs pasted as commands); the reference reads it as a word.

Bash reads a parameter expansion up to its closing brace and reports a bad substitution only when the line runs; bash 5.2 with -n accepts every line of this family (nested ${${x}}, unknown operators such as ${x:Dall}). Version 6 reads it as bash does; an expansion with no parameter name at all stays invalid.

Bash only warns when a here-document is not ended by its delimiter and takes the rest of the input as the document; version 6 refuses the line, since text meant as commands would otherwise be read as data.
A Makefile variable such as $< is a $ followed by a redirect with no target; bash 5.2 rejects the line with a syntax error, as version 6 does.
Version 6 does not support the (( )) arithmetic command and refuses it whole; the reference reads this one as nested subshells.
A backtick substitution inside another needs its own escaping rules; version 6 refuses it as unsupported rather than guess which command runs.

Each line was checked one by one with real bash 5.2 (bash -n): bash reads it without a syntax error, as version 6 does (&> redirects, let without arguments, jq and Python lines that are odd but valid words, $((...)[0]) in PowerShell lines). Listed by opaque id, so no other line is excused.
A backslash at the end of a comment does not continue the line: bash 5.2 runs the next line as its own command, so version 6's two parts are right where the reference joins them into one.
